translation: Aristotle, and likewise Theophrastus, have stated precisely what one must look to in order to suppose a nature to be well-tempered or ill-tempered; but these people do not even know this. Rather, when they hear them saying that the animal is moist and warm, or that the mixture of the child is moist and warm, they neither understand how these things have been said, and they recklessly transfer the account to the seasons, as though it were the same thing, or not far different, for one's proper mixture to be moist and warm and for that of the air surrounding us to be so. For it is not the same, nor is a mixture of an animal called moist and warm in the same way as a moist and warm mixture of air. What the cause of all these things was I shall now explain, and I shall show clearly to those willing to pay attention how small slips in the

the same, or to evacuate the moisture of something dispersed in certain spaces, or to render its proper mixture drier. For an uneven dyscrasia arises in inflamed parts, the homoeomerous bodies not yet having departed from their proper nature but still being changed and altered, while all the spaces between them are filled with the flux. All things, then, that are warm and moist in mixture, when applied to parts so disposed, evacuate that superfluity which has occupied the spaces between the homoeomerous parts, but the bodies themselves they are so far from drying that they even impart moisture to them. That, then, is how the truth stands; but what has been said requires demonstration, which, thinking it too long to be added in this treatise, and moreover requiring a hearer versed in the power of drugs, I defer; at any rate

and with rose cerate it helps greatly. For these conditions too many other drugs will be described in the following discourse, some having a power similar to the palm plaster, some even more drastic. But for fluxional conditions this is the best drug of all, and it has often accomplished something beyond hope. Once, then, when a thigh had suppurated near the groin, while the inflammation throughout it was unconcocted, the leg was positioned by us so that the ichors would flow out towards the groin; and since this went on at the wound that had formed for a longer time, the flux that had descended into the thigh was evacuated, but a fistulous condition arose under the skin throughout the whole thigh, so that I wished to incise it near the kneecap, so that on either side there might be an outlet for the ichors

concerning nourishment, as the bad and the not bad are spoken of in the category of relation, and evidently also the harmful and the beneficial. For in another sense you might say that the Attalic is better than this plaster, in that that one is more widely useful. Indeed Asclepiades himself, writing next after this one just mentioned that very one made with white pepper, does not name it Attalic but Pamphilian, being ignorant, I think, of the man who first discovered it, and adding the name of the one who used it and gave it to him. Its promise he wrote word for word thus: Another, called the Pamphilian, a successful drug; it acts on old and hard-to-heal [ulcers], carbuncles, epinyctides, achores, psoric conditions; it glues sinuses together; it acts on abscesses, condylomata, and the drug is almost more widely useful. He says it is composed of white lead

each of these precisely; let it be for the sake of contributing something to the whiteness of the drug. About white lead too it has been said before, and about the oil and the manner of boiling and the surrounding air and the fire, how each of them would contribute something to the whiteness. And just as in the other cases, so also in these, one must know the powers of water and vinegar and sea water and of the whitest wine, and mix in the composition what is most useful for the condition being treated. For in callous ulcers, which have thick and hard lips and need much thinning, those triturated with vinegar and sea water are more useful than those with water; but in those where the moisture carried into the ulcers is acrid and biting, they should rather be triturated in water

each of the metallic substances, just as, again, rather in wine in those in which the moisture flowing onto the ulcers appears abundant. Each, then, of those I have named, triturated in each of the said liquids for many days, I threw in each time into the drugs made with white lead and litharge, and found by test that all of them cicatrize excellently; and I also gave some recipes to friends who needed such drugs, by whom too, when brought to trial, they were seen to keep their promise. So when the litharge has been boiled beforehand with the white lead, as has been said, and the drug has come near to the non-soiling consistency, one must add some of the larch or the terebinth resin with the white wax, and when these are well united, add the metallic substances, having this proportion: of the litharge and the white lead, as usual, a litra of each with two litrai of oil; let it be boiled many times

but if something of its inflammation should remain scirrhous, to apply one of the things that dry sufficiently. Since, then, something seemed to be lacking, I first used the drug made with the root of dracontium, which in other respects has the same as the Egyptian drug called Isis, but has taken in addition the root of dracontium; next after this, having used the one called Athena, from that I went on finally to the cicatrizing drugs. In another case, anointing the denuded parts of the wound with the pastille dissolved in boiled must, I laid on externally euphorbium mixed with wax and resin in such quantity that it became at once plaster-like and preserved the power of the euphorbium. How one, looking to these aims, might compose the drug I shall tell next; for indeed I also made another drug with vinegar

as with resin and pitch. For this reason I mix with the cerate resin or pitch or a part of each. It is clear, then, that when these are mixed in, the oil is no longer to be put in equal to them; for wax needs much fat for moistness, but of the resins the entirely dry need little, while the moist even want to take in some dry substance for a plaster-like consistency. Among waxes, then, the difference in moistness and dryness is not great, but in resins, conversely, as also in pitch, the difference of the dry from the moist is very great. The driest of the resins, then, is the one some call roasted, others Colophonian; second is that from the potteries, unpurified and unroasted; but if one purifies it

you have seen me doing constantly, not only with this but also with the ammoniac incense. The drug written after this one by the Tarantine is also of the same promise, in this proportion: chalcitis 25 dr., cadmia 12 dr.; having ground them separately and mixed them, pour on unadulterated wine, boiled, so that they are kneaded moderately; then grind until it dries; and having melted wax 50 dr., terebinth resin 30 dr., myrtle oil 8 kotylai, mix into the cerate 20 dr. of the dry ingredients. This drug too has nothing of the softening ones; but in the mixing with the cerate, one trained rationally in the methods I set out would suitably produce the quantity of the mixture appropriate for each of the ulcers. And well too [is] the unadulterated wine, that is, that with which sea water has not been mixed

the meltables, having let them cool somewhat, sprinkle the dry ingredients on them, stirring carefully. You must have myrrh, frankincense, bdellium, opopanax triturated with vinegar; and the contents of the dish are thrown onto these and ground so that wax lumps do not form. When it is in good condition, take it up into a wooden box, having first smeared it with iris oil. On the third class of hard-to-cure ulcers, about which Asclepiades wrote these words verbatim: For ulcers that do not close at all, or close but break open again, either because the flesh is corrupted or because the underlying bones have decayed, one must use the preparations set out below. For chironian and hard-to-heal ulcers, a successful drug: scale of copper, scraped verdigris, 1 oz. each; wax half a litra; larch resin 1 1/2 oz.; [pour] the meltables onto the dry ingredients, take up and use, softening carefully and laying a small spread dressing over it, at

the metallic substances with vinegar, and after that adding the dry ingredients and grinding again; then, when these have a mud-like consistency, mixing in the meltables as said before. Another: asphalt, terebinth resin and Bruttian pitch, 1 litra each; oil 24 dr.; litharge, white lead, manna, verdigris, scale and opopanax, of each an amount equal to the twenty-four drachms of the oil; ladanum 2 oz., that is 16 dr.; and two kotylai of vinegar. This drug too is prepared in the same way as the two before it. Another: chrysocolla, scale and stomoma, 4 dr. each; of verdigris and chalcanthum half of each, that is 2 dr. each; wax 25 dr., that is 3 oz. and one drachm; terebinth resin 2 oz., that is 16 dr.; melt the wax with the terebinth

Of rust of copper and Indian aloe, of burnt copper and good diphryges, sixteen and a half of each ingredient; twenty drachms and 4 of galbanum; of manna and frankincense equal amounts, twice 12; of ammoniacum twice 5 and twice 20; sixteen drachms of Attic propolis; of long birthwort twice 10 drachms; twice 6 drachms of the scale of Cyprian copper; and of the driest gentian root an equal amount. To all these add of the herb dittany, dry and having its flower, 20 holkai, ground fine. Putting litharge with oil into a new, earthenware, wide-mouthed dish, boil on a light and gentle fire, stirring with a spatula, until it gets the thickness of Attic honey. Adding again an equal amount of the scale, boil more vigorously; then, when the drug has become tawny, add the copper and the diphryges; making the drug non-soiling and set, add the wax and the

wax, having neither of these, but the ammoniac incense alone, thrown in, will make the drug parched. But for plaster-making (for it is no worse to name it so) both the wax and the resin are useful; for softening and dispersing belong to the drug from the ammoniac alone, which is foremost among the emollients and a rival also to the discutients. Recalling what was said in the fifth book of On the Power of Simple Drugs, of what sort the mixture must be for such drugs, you will need no further new teaching. For the primary active powers in drugs lie in heat and coldness and moisture and dryness; secondary are the emollient, the discutient, the repellent, the attractive, the concoctive, the detergent and the septic, just as also

of all, carefully; again let a little drip off; if you see it well-coloured and blended, lift the pot at once from the fire, and add galbanum softened beforehand. If the drug is much too hard, add oil to it for a good temper. Thus straining it, then into another vessel, knead it cold with the hands and so store it away. I shall write out another of the same kind as the one before this. It acts on the affections I named before. Better than all drugs this one cicatrizes ulcers hard-to-heal, callous and chronic; the eruptions arising on the face this one treats without any bad biting; seats that have fissures and indurations, the condylomatous ones and calluses it removes. Prepare it thus: a mna of good litharge (a mna is a litra and a third part of a litra); of good Pontic wax half a mna; of verdigris a fourth part of a mna, good, scraped

scrofulous swellings, reducing every oedema, and healing the watery conditions of liver or spleen, bringing on abundant excretions of urine, and it resolves chronic sciaticas. Using this, Ulpianus, a gifted young man, helped very many. It has one litra of Pontic wax, one of roasted [resin] and one of the pine [resin], of fresh quicklime one ounce, of split alum one ounce, equal to one of these of Pontic arsenic. Pouring on these a little fragrant vinegar, grind sufficiently in a larger mortar; adding to the wax and resin a little oil, having melted it over a fire of vigorous flame, and mixing all carefully and making soft masses, making it the thickness of a non-soiling one, keep it in store, using it where needed on a fresh compress. Kratistos, the father of the drug, also said that for the relief of long diseases

which also heal small inflammations. Of the compound emollients some are, as one might say, weaker, in the first rank; some not much stronger than these, in the second; and some others in the third, and besides these others in the fourth. One should use them, as was said before, for slight indurations and soft bodies, those of the first rank; for those stronger than these, both bodies and affections, those of the second; just as also those of the third and of the fourth proportionally. They write out also those of each of them separately.
